claim: Hyperplasia of sympathoadrenal cell precursors during embryogenesis in Nf1-deficient mice is independent of Nf1's role in down-modulating RAS-MAPK signaling.
source: Earlier reports showed that hyperplasia of sympathoadrenal cell precursors during embryogenesis in Nf1-deficient mice is independent of Nf1's role in down-modulating RAS-MAPK signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to earlier reports in the literature.

claim: nf1 loss leads to aberrant activation of RAS signaling in MYCN-induced neuroblastomas in zebrafish.
source: We demonstrate in zebrafish that nf1 loss leads to aberrant activation of RAS signaling in MYCN-induced neuroblastomas that arise in these precursors
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically immunohistochemistry showing increased pERK, pAKT, and pS6 in nf1-deficient neuroblastomas (Figure 6).

claim: The GTPase-activating protein (GAP)-related domain (GRD) is sufficient to suppress the acceleration of neuroblastoma in nf1-deficient fish.
source: the GTPase-activating protein (GAP)-related domain (GRD) is sufficient to suppress the acceleration of neuroblastoma in nf1-deficient fish
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that expression of wild-type GRD significantly reduced neuroblastoma penetrance in nf1-deficient fish (Figure 7).

claim: The GRD domain does not suppress the hypertrophy of sympathoadrenal cells in nf1 mutant embryos.
source: but not the hypertrophy of sympathoadrenal cells in nf1 mutant embryos
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that GRD expression did not rescue SCG overgrowth in nf1 mutant embryos (Figure 1H).

claim: NF1 relies on a different mechanism to suppress malignant transformation than it does to modulate normal neural crest cell growth.
source: Thus, even though neuroblastoma is a classical "developmental tumor", NF1 relies on a very different mechanism to suppress malignant transformation than it does to modulate normal neural crest cell growth.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of GRD on tumor suppression versus developmental overgrowth.

claim: There is marked synergy in tumor cell killing between MEK inhibitors (trametinib) and retinoids (isotretinoin) in primary nf1a-/- zebrafish neuroblastomas.
source: We also show marked synergy in tumor cell killing between MEK inhibitors (trametinib) and retinoids (isotretinoin) in primary nf1a-/- zebrafish neuroblastomas.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing synergistic effects by isobologram analysis (Figure 8).

claim: Neuroblastoma is the most common noncranial solid tumor in childhood, accounting for 8–10% of all childhood malignancies and 15% of all cancer deaths in children.
source: This cancer is the most common noncranial solid tumor in childhood, accounting for 8–10% of all childhood malignancies and 15% of all cancer deaths in children (Maris and Matthay, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Maris and Matthay, 1999).

claim: Neuroblastoma is genetically heterogeneous, with multiple interacting genetic mutations required to generate fully transformed malignant tumors.
source: Neuroblastoma is genetically heterogeneous, with multiple interacting genetic mutations required to generate fully transformed malignant tumors.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about neuroblastoma genetics.

claim: Resequencing studies have documented a very low frequency of somatic mutations in neuroblastoma.
source: As in many other pediatric cancers, resequencing studies have documented a very low frequency of somatic mutations in neuroblastoma (Cheung et al., 2012; Molenaar et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple resequencing studies.

claim: ALK mutations occur in approximately 9.2% of neuroblastoma cases.
source: including ALK (~9.2% of cases)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to resequencing studies (Cheung et al., 2012; Molenaar et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2013).

claim: PTPN11 mutations occur in approximately 2.9% of neuroblastoma cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to resequencing studies (Cheung et al., 2012; Molenaar et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2013).

claim: ATRX mutations occur in approximately 2.5% of neuroblastoma cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to resequencing studies (Cheung et al., 2012; Molenaar et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2013).

claim: NF1 mutations occur in approximately 1% of neuroblastoma cases.
source: and NF1 (~1%)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to resequencing studies (Cheung et al., 2012; Molenaar et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2013).

claim: Amplification and overexpression of the MYCN oncogene occurs in about one-third of neuroblastoma patients and is a principal indicator of a poor prognosis.
source: Amplification and overexpression of the MYCN oncogene occurs in about one-third of patients and is a principal indicator of a poor prognosis (Brodeur et al., 1984; Hansford et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brodeur et al., 1984; Hansford et al., 2004).

claim: Genomic aberrations that inactivate the NF1 tumor suppressor gene have been identified in 6% of primary neuroblastomas and are predictive of a poor outcome.
source: Genomic aberrations that inactivate the NF1 tumor suppressor gene, including loss-of-function mutations and deletions, as well as decreased expression levels of the gene, have been identified in 6% of primary neuroblastomas and are predictive of a poor outcome (Hölzel et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hölzel et al., 2010).

claim: The NF1 gene encodes neurofibromin, a 2818 amino acid protein whose main functional domain is the ~330 amino acid GTPase-activating protein-related domain (GRD).
source: The NF1 gene encodes neurofibromin, a 2818 amino acid protein whose main functional domain is the ~330 amino acid GTPase-activating protein-related domain (GRD)
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the NF1 protein structure.

claim: The GRD domain negatively regulates RAS signaling by catalyzing the hydrolysis of RAS-GTP into RAS-GDP.
source: which negatively regulates RAS signaling by catalyzing the hydrolysis of RAS-GTP into RAS-GDP (Nur-E-Kamal et al., 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Nur-E-Kamal et al., 1993).

claim: One consequence of NF1 loss is the aberrant activation of RAS signaling.
source: thus, one consequence of NF1 loss is the aberrant activation of RAS signaling (Maertens and Cichowski, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Maertens and Cichowski, 2014).

claim: Loss of NF1 in neuroblastoma cells mediates resistance to retinoic acid via hyperactive RAS signaling, which can be abolished by enforced expression of NF1-GRD.
source: Loss of NF1 in neuroblastoma cells has been shown to mediate resistance to retinoic acid via hyperactive RAS signaling, which can be abolished by enforced expression of NF1-GRD (Hölzel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hölzel et al., 2010).

claim: Nf1 mutant mice die at birth with evidence of massive overgrowth of neural crest tissues, including the sympathetic ganglia.
source: However, it is known that NF1 has other functions in PSNS development besides the downmodulation of RAS signaling, because Nf1 mutant mice die at birth with evidence of massive overgrowth of neural crest tissues, including the sympathetic ganglia
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Ismat et al., 2006).

claim: Overexpression of the GRD domain is unable to reverse the overgrowth of sympathetic ganglia in Nf1 mutant mice.
source: while overexpression of the GRD domain is unable to reverse this overgrowth (Ismat et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Ismat et al., 2006).

claim: Studies showed identical or only modestly elevated RAS-GTP levels in NF1-deficient human neuroblastoma cells, in contrast to highly elevated RAS-GTP levels in NF1-deficient Schwannoma tumor cells.
source: In addition, studies showed identical or only modestly elevated RAS-GTP levels in NF1-deficient human neuroblastoma cells, in contrast to highly elevated RAS-GTP levels in NF1-deficient Schwannoma tumor cells (Johnson et al., 1993; The et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Johnson et al., 1993; The et al., 1993).

claim: Numerous mutations of NF1 cause neurofibromatosis type 1 but do not appear to affect protein stability or GAP function.
source: These results, coupled with the numerous mutations of NF1 that cause the disease neurofibromatosis type 1, but do not appear to affect protein stability or GAP function (Abernathy et al., 1997; Fahsold et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Abernathy et al., 1997; Fahsold et al., 2000).

claim: Functional domains outside the GRD may mediate important aspects of neurofibromin function in neuroblastoma tumor suppression.
source: argue that functional domains outside the GRD may mediate important aspects of neurofibromin function in neuroblastoma tumor suppression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the evidence about NF1 mutations and RAS-GTP levels.

claim: Complete loss of nf1 led to increased cell numbers in the superior cervical ganglia (SCG) at 6 days postfertilization.
source: As in the mouse, complete loss of nf1 led to increased cell numbers in the SCG at 6 dpf (compare Figure 1D with panel A, also panel E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Homozygous loss of nf1a led to the same level of increase in SCG neuronal cell number as homozygous loss of nf1a plus nf1b.
source: Homozygous loss of nf1a led to the same level of increase in SCG neuronal cell number as homozygous loss of nf1a plus nf1b
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and G.

claim: The loss of nf1b had little effect on SCG cell numbers.
source: while the loss of nf1b had little effect on SCG cell numbers (Figure 1B and G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: nf1a is expressed at a much higher level than nf1b in sympathetic neurons as well as the whole embryo during the first week of zebrafish embryonic development.
source: which is consistent with the fact that nf1a is expressed at a much higher level than nf1b in sympathetic neurons as well as the whole embryo during the first week of zebrafish embryonic development (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At 3, 4 and 6 weeks of life, the expression levels of nf1a and nf1b were similar to each other, without evidence of the predominance of nf1a that was observed at 1 week of age.
source: Later in development at 3, 4 and 6 weeks of life, we observed lower relative nf1a and nf1b levels in RNA from the whole fish, and at these time points the expression levels of nf1a and nf1b were similar to each other, without evidence of the predominance of nf1a that was observed at 1 week of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The functionally active wild-type GRD domain did not rescue SCG overgrowth in nf1 mutant fish.
source: In agreement with studies in the mouse, we found that the functionally active wild-type GRD domain (designated 'wt-GRD') did not rescue SCG overgrowth in nf1 mutant fish, as the levels of SCG overgrowth in nf1a-/-; nf1b+/+;EGFP embryos transgenic for dbh:wt-GRD;dbh:mCherry were similar to those of nf1a-/-; nf1b+/+;EGFP embryos at 6 dpf (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: nf1 is required to control the growth of PSNS precursor cells during embryologic development in zebrafish as well as mice.
source: Thus, nf1 is required to control the growth of PSNS precursor cells during embryologic development in zebrafish as well as mice
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from zebrafish and comparison with published mouse studies.

claim: The GAP-independent activities of NF1 restrict the growth of normal neural crest-derived tissues during development in zebrafish as well as in mice.
source: and this activity is independent of the nf1 GRD in zebrafish as well as in mice.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing GRD does not rescue developmental overgrowth.

claim: Loss of Nf1 increases the penetrance of MYCN-induced neuroblastoma in MYCN transgenic mice.
source: Loss of Nf1 has been shown to increase the penetrance of MYCN-induced neuroblastoma in MYCN transgenic mice (Weiss et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Weiss et al., 1997).

claim: Transgenic fish lines that expressed EGFP in the PSNS but not the MYCN transgene did not develop neuroblastoma, regardless of the mutational status of nf1.
source: Transgenic fish lines that expressed EGFP in the PSNS but not the MYCN transgene did not develop neuroblastoma, regardless of the mutational status of nf1, indicating that loss of up to three alleles of nf1 was insufficient to induce neuroblastoma on its own (Figure 2A and Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 4C.

claim: Loss of up to three alleles of nf1 was insufficient to induce neuroblastoma on its own.
source: indicating that loss of up to three alleles of nf1 was insufficient to induce neuroblastoma on its own (Figure 2A and Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no tumors in EGFP-only fish with nf1 mutations.

claim: Over the 20-week course of the experiment, neuroblastoma developed in one of the 14 transgenic MYCN-positive zebrafish with wild-type nf1 alleles.
source: Over the 20-week course of this experiment, neuroblastoma developed in one of the 14 transgenic MYCN-positive zebrafish with wild-type nf1 alleles (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The first tumors arose in the interrenal gland (IRG) of 4-week-old animals with loss of one or more of the nf1a alleles, representing the earliest onset observed in this MYCN transgenic model.
source: The first tumors arose in the interrenal gland (IRG) of 4-week-old animals with loss of one or more of the nf1a alleles, representing the earliest onset we have observed in this MYCN transgenic model (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The tumor masses that developed in MYCN transgenic fish with nf1 mutations consisted of small, undifferentiated tumor cells with distinct single nucleoli, which were diagnostic of neuroblastoma.
source: Histopathologically, the tumor masses that developed in MYCN transgenic fish with nf1 mutations consisted of small, undifferentiated tumor cells with distinct single nucleoli (Figure 2B), which were diagnostic of neuroblastoma
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The tumors in MYCN transgenic fish with nf1 mutations were indistinguishable from the tumors that develop in MYCN transgenic zebrafish with wild-type nf1 alleles.
source: and indistinguishable from the tumors that develop in MYCN transgenic zebrafish with wild-type nf1 alleles (Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological comparison and citation to previous work (Zhu et al., 2012).

claim: Three genotypes that retained two copies of functional nf1a were associated with similar tumor onsets, with a neuroblastoma penetrance of ~5.5%.
source: Three genotypes that retained two copies of functional nf1a were associated with similar tumor onsets, as shown in blue in Figure 2C, with a neuroblastoma penetrance of ~5.5%
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of nf1b has much less impact than nf1a on the pathogenesis of neuroblastoma in the PSNS.
source: suggesting that loss of nf1b has much less impact than nf1a on the pathogenesis of neuroblastoma in the PSNS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the tumor penetrance data in different genotypes.

claim: The highest neuroblastoma penetrance levels at 4 weeks of age (82.6%) was observed in MYCN transgenic fish with homozygous loss of nf1a and heterozygous loss of nf1b.
source: By contrast, the highest neuroblastoma penetrance levels at 4 weeks of age (82.6%) was observed in MYCN transgenic fish with homozygous loss of nf1a and heterozygous loss of nf1b, which produced the earliest onset and highest penetrance of neuroblastoma that we have observed in this model system.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the tumor watch experiment.

claim: The penetrance of nf1a-/- fish with wild-type nf1b was 62.5%.
source: Finally, the penetrance of nf1a-/- fish with wild-type nf1b was still very high at 62.5%
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the tumor watch experiment.

claim: Of the two paralogues, the nf1a gene is primarily responsible for tumor suppression in the developing zebrafish sympathetic nervous system.
source: indicating that of the two paralogues, the nf1a gene is primarily responsible for tumor suppression in the developing zebrafish sympathetic nervous system.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential tumor penetrance data between nf1a and nf1b mutants.

claim: Neuroblastomas that arose in fish with nf1a+/-;nf1b+/+;EGFP;MYCN and nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;EGFP;MYCN genotypes were all strongly immunoreactive for tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and the pan-neuronal marker Hu.
source: Neuroblastomas that arose in fish with nf1a+/-;nf1b+/+;EGFP;MYCN and nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;EGFP;MYCN genotypes were all strongly immunoreactive for tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and the pan-neuronal marker Hu, comparable to the fish with wild-type nf1 alleles (nf1a+/+;nf1b+/+;EGFP;MYCN; Figure 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The neuroblastomas are derived from sympathetic neuroblast precursors (TH+, Hu+).
source: indicating derivation from sympathetic neuroblast precursors (TH+, Hu+).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunohistochemistry marker expression pattern.

claim: MYCN-induced neuroblastoma tumors arise from adrenal sympathetic neuroblasts that are prevented from differentiation into chromaffin cells by the overexpression of MYCN.
source: This is consistent with our previous report in nf1 wild-type fish that MYCN-induced neuroblastoma tumors arise from adrenal sympathetic neuroblasts that are prevented from differentiation into chromaffin cells by the overexpression of MYCN (Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Zhu et al., 2012) and consistency with current findings.

claim: Predominately TH+, Hu- chromaffin cells were detected in the IRG of nf1a mutant fish lacking MYCN overexpression.
source: Predominately TH+, Hu- chromaffin cells were detected in the IRG of nf1a mutant fish lacking MYCN overexpression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of nf1 alone does not contribute to developmental arrest of PSNS neuroblasts at the TH+, Hu+ stage.
source: indicating that loss of nf1 alone does not contribute to developmental arrest of PSNS neuroblasts at the TH+, Hu+ stage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that nf1 mutant fish without MYCN have chromaffin cells, not arrested neuroblasts.

claim: Loss of nf1a synergizes with overexpression of MYCN in the initiation of neuroblastoma.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that loss of nf1a synergizes with overexpression of MYCN in the initiation of neuroblastoma
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on tumor penetrance and timing.

claim: Loss of nf1a is insufficient to initiate neuroblastoma on its own.
source: but that loss of nf1a is insufficient to initiate neuroblastoma on its own
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no tumors in nf1a mutant fish without MYCN.

claim: Loss of nf1a by itself does not lead to a block of terminal differentiation in PSNS neuroblasts in the IRG.
source: possibly because loss of nf1a by itself does not lead to a block of terminal differentiation in PSNS neuroblasts in the IRG.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that nf1a mutant fish without MYCN have differentiated chromaffin cells.

claim: Expansion of EGFP+ sympathoadrenal cells was observed in the IRG of nf1a heterozygous zebrafish (nf1a+/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP), with an average increased expansion of 1.73 fold by the end of the 3-week period.
source: Expansion of EGFP+ sympathoadrenal cells was observed in the IRG of nf1a heterozygous zebrafish (nf1a+/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP, Figure 4A middle panel), with an average increased expansion of 1.73 fold by the end of the 3-week period
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The tumor induction rate in nf1a+/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish was 43% (9/21 fish had tumors before they reached 6 weeks of age).
source: and a tumor induction rate of 43% (9/21 fish had tumors before they reached 6 weeks of age; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The EGFP+ sympathoadrenal cells in the IRG of nf1a-/- homozygous zebrafish expanded with an average 6.61-fold expansion rate within the 3 week period (nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+; MYCN;EGFP).
source: By contrast, the EGFP+ sympathoadrenal cells in the IRG of nf1a-/- homozygous zebrafish expanded much more rapidly, with an average 6.61-fold expansion rate within the 3 week period (nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+; MYCN;EGFP)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tumor development occurred in 9 of 10 nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish before 6 weeks of age.
source: and tumor development in 9 of 10 fish before 6 weeks of age (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The loss of nf1a promotes MYCN-induced neuroblastoma onset and progression in vivo in zebrafish in a dose-dependent manner.
source: These data demonstrate that the loss of nf1a promotes MYCN-induced neuroblastoma onset and progression in vivo in zebrafish in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential expansion rates in heterozygous versus homozygous nf1a mutants.

claim: Wild-type zebrafish transgenic for MYCN exhibit hyperplasia of sympathetic neuroblast precursors in the IRG from 3 to 5 weeks of life, followed by a developmentally-timed apoptotic response.
source: Wild-type zebrafish transgenic for MYCN exhibit hyperplasia of sympathetic neuroblast precursors in the IRG from 3 to 5 weeks of life, followed by a developmentally-timed apoptotic response, resulting in regression of the hyperplastic sympathoadrenal cells in most fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Zhu et al., 2012) and current observations.

claim: The developmentally-timed apoptotic response results in regression of the hyperplastic sympathoadrenal cells in most MYCN transgenic fish.
source: resulting in regression of the hyperplastic sympathoadrenal cells in most fish.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the low tumor penetrance in wild-type MYCN fish.

claim: The low penetrance and relatively long latency of tumors in wild-type MYCN fish is due to the apoptotic response, with tumors developing in 5-15% of animals at 12 to 20 weeks.
source: This leads to a low penetrance, with tumors developing in 515% of animals, and a relatively long latency of 12 to 20 weeks (Figure 2C) (Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work (Zhu et al., 2012).

claim: Positive staining for cleaved caspase-3 was observed at 6 weeks of age in nf1 wild-type MYCN transgenic fish.
source: In the current study, we observed positive staining for cleaved caspase-3 at 6 weeks of age in nf1 wild-type MYCN transgenic fish, consistent with our previous findings
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cleaved caspase-3 was not detected in the IRG of either nf1a+/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP or nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish.
source: but we did not detect staining for cleaved caspase-3 in the IRG of either nf1a+/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP or nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Loss of either one or both alleles of nf1a blocked the apoptotic response due to overexpression of MYCN in sympathetic neuroblasts.
source: Thus, loss of either one or both alleles of nf1a blocked the apoptotic response due to overexpression of MYCN in sympathetic neuroblasts, thus promoting tumor cell survival and leading to the development of neuroblastoma at high penetrance (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of cleaved caspase-3 staining and high tumor penetrance.

claim: The effects of loss of NF1 on cell survival appear similar to the effects of mutational activation of the ALK tyrosine kinase.
source: The effects of loss of NF1 on cell survival therefore appear similar to the effects of mutational activation of the ALK tyrosine kinase (Zhu et al., 2012), which also promotes activated signaling through the RAS pathway.
evidence: This claim is based on inference and comparison with previous work on ALK (Zhu et al., 2012).

claim: Neuroblastomas arising in the nf1a+/- and nf1a-/- background exhibited a progressively higher percentage of nuclei with PCNA staining (30% for nf1a+/- and 80% for nf1a-/-) compared to PCNA staining of 20% of nuclei in the wild-type nf1a+/+ genotype.
source: We found that neuroblastomas arising in the nf1a+/- and nf1a-/- background exhibited a progressively higher percentage of nuclei with PCNA staining (30% for nf1a+/- and 80% for nf1a-/-) compared to PCNA staining of 20% of nuclei in the wild-type nf1a+/+ genotype (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: Loss of nf1a resulted in an increased neuroblastoma cell proliferative fraction.
source: Thus, loss of nf1a resulted in an increased neuroblastoma cell proliferative fraction, consistent with the observation that neuroblastoma tumors grow much more rapidly in fish with homozygous loss of nf1a (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from PCNA staining data and tumor growth kinetics.

claim: The tumor suppressor nf1 plays an important role in restricting both the proliferative rate and survival of MYCN-overexpressing hyperplastic sympathetic neuroblast precursors.
source: Together, our results support an important role of the tumor suppressor nf1 in restricting both the proliferative rate and survival of MYCN-overexpressing hyperplastic sympathetic neuroblast precursors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on apoptosis and proliferation.

claim: No significant differences in mRNA levels of cell cycle genes (ccna1, ccna2, ccnb1, ccnd1, ccnd2, ccnd3, ccne, cdk2, cdk4, cdk6 and e2f1) were detected between nf1a+/+;nf1b+/+;MYCN and nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN zebrafish tumors.
source: We did not detect significant differences in mRNA levels of these genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IRG of wild-type nf1a+/+;nf1b+/+;EGFP fish did not exhibit detectable phosphorylated ERK (pERK), phosphorylated AKT (pAKT) or phosphorylated S6 (pS6).
source: The IRG of wild-type nf1a+/+;nf1b+/+;EGFP fish did not exhibit detectable phosphorylated ERK (pERK), phosphorylated AKT (pAKT) or phosphorylated S6 (pS6), demonstrating a very low level of basal RAS activity in the normal sympathoadrenal cells of the IRG (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Notable increases in pERK, pAKT or pS6 were not observed in the nontransformed IRG of nf1a mutant fish that lacked MYCN overexpression.
source: We did not observe notable increases in pERK, pAKT or pS6 in the nontransformed IRG of nf1a mutant fish that lacked MYCN overexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of nf1 did not cause a detectable increase in the basal levels of endogenous RAS signaling in normal sympathoadrenal cells of the IRG.
source: Thus, the loss of nf1 did not cause a detectable increase in the basal levels of endogenous RAS signaling in normal sympathoadrenal cells of the IRG
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of increased phosphorylation of RAS pathway markers.

claim: In the absence of MYCN overexpression, sympathoadrenal cells rapidly differentiate into mature chromaffin cells.
source: probably because in the absence of MYCN overexpression they rapidly differentiate into mature chromaffin cells (Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and citation to previous work (Zhu et al., 2012).

claim: High levels of pERK, pAKT and pS6 were detected in neuroblastomas from 6-week-old wild-type nf1a+/+; nf1b+/+;MYCN fish.
source: By immunohistochemistry and measurement of the area of the diaminobenzidine-peroxidase (DAB)-stained tumor cells, we detected high levels of pERK, pAKT and pS6 in neuroblastomas from 6-week-old fish (Figure 6A,D,G and J)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: RAS effector pathways are activated in the proliferating neuroblasts of wild-type nf1a+/+; nf1b+/+;MYCN fish that were blocked from terminal differentiation by overexpression of MYCN.
source: indicating activation of RAS effector pathways in the proliferating neuroblasts of wild-type nf1a+/+; nf1b+/+;MYCN fish that were blocked from terminal differentiation by overexpression of MYCN.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the detection of phosphorylated RAS pathway markers in MYCN-overexpressing tumors.

claim: Much higher levels of activation of RAS effector pathways were observed in neuroblastomas arising in nf1a-deficient fish, determined by significant increases of positive DAB-stained tumor areas.
source: In this context, it is not surprising that we observed much higher levels of activation of these effector pathways in neuroblastomas arising in nf1a-deficient fish, determined by significant increases of positive DAB-stained tumor areas (Figure 6 B,C,E,F,H,I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 6.

claim: The overexpression of MYCN blocks the differentiation of sympathoadrenal precursor cells, leaving them vulnerable to the potentiating effects of nf1 loss on RAS pathway activation.
source: Thus, the overexpression of MYCN blocks the differentiation of sympathoadrenal precursor cells, leaving them vulnerable to the potentiating effects of nf1 loss on RAS pathway activation, which in turn leads to the marked increased in neuroblastoma penetrance and growth rate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined effects of MYCN and nf1 loss on RAS signaling and tumor development.

claim: Inactivation of the NF1 gene in human neuroblastoma and melanoma cell lines does not result in increased levels of the GTP-bound form of Ras compared to similar lines that express normal levels of the NF1 protein.
source: We and others have shown that inactivation of the NF1 gene in human neuroblastoma and melanoma cell lines does not result in increased levels of the GTP-bound form of Ras compared to similar lines that express normal levels of the NF1 protein (Johnson et al., 1993; The et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Johnson et al., 1993; The et al., 1993).

claim: Loss of NF1 is one of a strikingly high frequency of diverse mutations that hyperactivate the RAS-MAPK signaling pathway in relapsed neuroblastoma.
source: However, a recent whole-genome sequencing study revealed that loss of NF1 is one of a strikingly high frequency of diverse mutations that hyperactivate the RAS-MAPK signaling pathway in relapsed neuroblastoma (Eleveld et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a whole-genome sequencing study (Eleveld et al., 2015).

claim: The inability to demonstrate increased GTP on RAS in NF1-deficient neuroblastoma cell lines may reflect the strong activation of the RAS-MAPK signaling pathway in essentially all high-risk neuroblastomas.
source: Thus, our inability to demonstrate increased GTP on RAS in NF1-deficient neuroblastoma cell lines may reflect the strong activation of the RAS-MAPK signaling pathway in essentially all high-risk neuroblastomas, if not by NF1 loss then by direct mutation of RAS itself or other types of mutations.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning to reconcile apparently contradictory findings.

claim: Neuroblastomas able to grow in vitro as continuous cell lines are invariably from patients with the very highest risk of treatment failure, and often are obtained from tumor biopsies at the time of relapse.
source: This interpretation becomes more appealing when one realizes that neuroblastomas able to grow in vitro as continuous cell lines are invariably from patients with the very highest risk of treatment failure, and often are obtained from tumor biopsies at the time of relapse.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about neuroblastoma cell line derivation.

claim: Most melanoma tumors harbor activating mutations in the RAS-MAPK pathway, including BRAF V600E and NRAS Q61L/R, as well as the loss of NF1 in a subset of cases.
source: The same relationship likely applies to melanoma cell lines as well, since most of these tumors harbor activating mutations in the RAS-MAPK pathway, including BRAF V600E and NRAS Q61L/R, as well as the loss of NF1 in a subset of cases (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Hodis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genomic studies (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Hodis et al., 2012).

claim: Studies of neural crest and PSNS development in Nf1 null mice were the first to implicate a GAP-independent activity of Nf1 in restricting the growth of sympathoadrenal cells.
source: Studies of neural crest and PSNS development in Nf1 null mice were the first to implicate a GAP-independent activity of Nf1 in restricting the growth of sympathoadrenal cells, as the GRD domain was not able to rescue the overgrowth of sympathetic neuroblasts in the adrenal medulla (Ismat et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published mouse studies (Ismat et al., 2006).

claim: Only 12 of 31 nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP;wt-GRD;mCherry fish developed neuroblastoma tumors by the age of 12 weeks (38.7%).
source: Only 12 of 31 nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP;wt-GRD;mCherry fish developed neuroblastoma tumors by the age of 12 weeks (38.7%, Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 35 of 41 nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish developed neuroblastoma tumors by the age of 12 weeks (85.4%).
source: compared to 35 of 41 nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish (85.4%, p<0.0001; Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Restoration of the NF1 GAP activity significantly reduced the penetrance of neuroblastoma in the nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP background.
source: indicating that restoration of the NF1 GAP activity significantly reduced the penetrance of neuroblastoma in the nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP background.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of tumor penetrance with and without wt-GRD expression.

claim: Stable expression of the inactive GRD R1276P mutant (designated 'mut-GRD') into nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish led to a frequency of neuroblastoma at 12 weeks of age that was identical to that in fish not transgenic for either GRD construct (90.0%).
source: As a control, we also stably expressed the inactive GRD R1276P mutant (designated 'mut-GRD') into nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish, which led to a frequency of neuroblastoma at 12 weeks of age that was identical to that in fish not transgenic for either GRD construct (90.0%, Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: NF1 normally suppresses the development of neuroblastoma by downmodulating oncogenic signals from RAS.
source: Because the GRD R1276P mutant specifically disrupts the ability of the GRD to mediate the NF1 GAP activity, this result indicates that NF1 normally suppresses the development of neuroblastoma by downmodulating oncogenic signals from RAS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of wild-type versus mutant GRD on tumor suppression.

claim: Even though a novel mechanism is responsible for restriction of PSNS neuron growth during normal embryogenesis, NF1 still acts as a classical GAP protein to suppress RAS-MAPK signaling for the suppression of neuroblastoma.
source: This finding stands in marked contrast to the inability of the same zebrafish line expressing the same level of GRD to rescue overgrowth of the SCG in normal development, indicating that even though a novel mechanism is responsible for restriction of PSNS neuron growth during normal embryogenesis, NF1 still acts as a classical GAP protein to suppress RAS-MAPK signaling for the suppression of neuroblastoma.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of GRD on development versus tumorigenesis.

claim: Only 2 of 58 neuroblastoma tumors in fish coinjected with the functionally active wt-GRD domain and the mCherry transgene exhibited mCherry fluorescence at 7 weeks of age (3.5%).
source: As shown in Figure 7B, D and F, only 2 of 58 neuroblastoma tumors in fish coinjected with the functionally active wt-GRD domain and the mCherry transgene exhibited mCherry fluorescence at 7 weeks of age (3.5%, Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mosaic transgenic fish shown in Figure 7.

claim: Coinjection of the mut-GRD domain and the mCherry transgene into nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish yielded strong mCherry fluorescence in 5 of 25 tumors that developed by 7 weeks of age (20.0%; p=0.0237).
source: By contrast, coinjection of the mut-GRD domain and the mCherry transgene into nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN;EGFP fish yielded strong mCherry fluorescence in 5 of 25 tumors that developed by 7 weeks of age (20.0%; p=0.0237; Figure 7B, D, and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mosaic transgenic fish shown in Figure 7.

claim: NF1 functions differently in normal development and tumorigenesis of the PSNS.
source: This experiment in primary injectants confirms our results in stable GRD transgenic lines, demonstrating that NF1 functions differently in normal development and tumorigenesis of the PSNS
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of GRD in development versus tumorigenesis.

claim: The tumor suppression function of NF1 in MYCN-induced neuroblastoma is mediated through the GAP activity of the GRD domain.
source: and the tumor suppression function of NF1 in MYCN-induced neuroblastoma is mediated through the GAP activity of the GRD domain.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments with wild-type versus mutant GRD.

claim: Trametinib significantly reduced the rate of tumor growth after 1 week of treatment, but did not by itself cause shrinkage of the tumor.
source: After 1 week of treatment with trametinib, we observed that the drug significantly reduced the rate of tumor growth, but did not by itself cause shrinkage of the tumor (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Isotretinoin alone leads to reduced tumor growth, with essentially stable tumor size over 7 days of treatment at the highest dosages.
source: In our nf1a-/-;nf1b+/+;MYCN; EGFP fish, isotretinoin alone leads to reduced tumor growth, with essentially stable tumor size over 7 days of treatment at the highest dosages (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The combination of isotretinoin and trametinib was much more active in reducing tumor size than either drug alone.
source: However, the combination of isotretinoin and trametinib was much more active in reducing tumor size, in many fish reducing the GFP fluorescence from the dβh promoter to the level of the normal IRG at 4 weeks of life (Figure 8A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Synergistic antitumor effects of trametinib and isotretinoin were documented in vivo at several different dosage combinations by isobologram analysis.
source: Importantly, synergistic antitumor effects of trametinib and isotretinoin were documented in vivo at several different dosage combinations by isobologram analysis (Figure 8B)
evidence: This claim is supported by isobologram analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Inhibition of RAS-MAPK signaling can significantly improve the treatment of very aggressive neuroblastoma when it is combined with the inhibition of other key pathways.
source: indicating that inhibition of RAS-MAPK signaling can significantly improve the treatment of this very aggressive form of neuroblastoma when it is combined with the inhibition of other key pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the synergistic drug effects observed.

claim: The nf1-deficient, MYCN-transgenic zebrafish model is one of a very few systems in which extensive analysis of the synergistic activity of two or more drugs can be evaluated in primary tumors in vivo.
source: Because of the very high penetrance and rapid onset of neuroblastoma in our nf1-deficient, MYCN-transgenic zebrafish model, it becomes one of a very few systems in which extensive analysis of the synergistic activity of two or more drugs can be evaluated in primary tumors in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the utility of the model system.

claim: There is recent evidence documenting the profound impact of RAS-MAPK hyperactivation in therapy-resistant neuroblastoma of childhood.
source: This capability is especially valuable given the recent evidence documenting the profound impact of RAS-MAPK hyperactivation in therapy-resistant neuroblastoma of childhood (Eleveld et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study (Eleveld et al., 2015).

claim: Mutations leading to activated RAS-MAPK signaling occur in nearly 80% of relapsed neuroblastomas.
source: The recent discovery that mutations leading to activated RAS-MAPK signaling occur in nearly 80% of relapsed neuroblastomas has clear implications for the selection of targeted therapy for this tumor (Eleveld et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study (Eleveld et al., 2015).

claim: MEK inhibitors and other agents targeting the RAS-MAPK pathway might suppress the outgrowth of resistant clones and therefore should be investigated as part of the initial combination therapy for high-risk neuroblastoma.
source: Indeed, it suggests that MEK inhibitors and other agents targeting the RAS-MAPK pathway might suppress the outgrowth of resistant clones and therefore should be investigated as part of the initial combination therapy for high-risk neuroblastoma.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic strategies based on the findings.

claim: The zebrafish model of MYCN-driven neuroblastoma with nf1 loss is ideally suited for the rapid in vivo analysis of the effects of candidate small-molecule inhibitors.
source: Our zebrafish model of MYCN-driven neuroblastoma with nf1 loss is ideally suited for the rapid in vivo analysis of the effects of candidate small-molecule inhibitors selected for this purpose.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the utility of the model system.

claim: Neuroblastomas can be detected in most MYCN-transgenic fish with nf1a loss by 3 weeks of age.
source: Neuroblastomas can be detected in most MYCN-transgenic fish with nf1a loss by 3 weeks of age, when the fish are very small, making it feasible to test the effectiveness of many drugs and drug combinations for their ability to kill primary neuroblastoma cells in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on tumor onset timing.

claim: Studies using the zebrafish model should be a valuable asset in devising new therapeutic strategies for neuroblastomas with mutations affecting the RAS-MAPK pathway.
source: Studies using our model should be a valuable asset in devising new therapeutic strategies for neuroblastomas with mutations affecting the RAS-MAPK pathway, which appear to be a major cause of relapse in children with this devastating tumor.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the potential value of the model system.

claim: Mutations affecting the RAS-MAPK pathway appear to be a major cause of relapse in children with neuroblastoma.
source: which appear to be a major cause of relapse in children with this devastating tumor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited literature about RAS-MAPK mutations in relapsed neuroblastoma.
